title: The Third Room
body:
Camp is quiet. Wren is not (she is never quiet), but tonight her chatter keeps circling something and landing short of it.

'Three washouts,' she says finally, holding up fingers. 'Evocation: bored. Wards: bored. But the third room.' The finger stays up a long time. 'Chronomantic theory. I wasn't bored, I was WRONG, and I never got to find out why. The examiner had my thesis on his desk the morning the sky tore. It's still there. Mid-grade. There's a frozen quill two inches above my margin.'

She looks at you the way people look at a door.

choices.label: Promise her the answer: the campus holds, and so does that desk
choices.resultText: 'Then it can still be graded,' she says, very softly, and starts planning like a woman with a fourth chance.

choices.label: Ask what the thesis argued
choices.resultText: 'That a held moment isn't stopped time. It's LONG time.' She laughs, badly. 'I got marked wrong in a world that is currently one enormous held moment. I want my points.'

title: The Third Room (Again)
body:
You have heard this confession before, in a year this world never had. So when Wren holds up three fingers and starts with 'Evocation: bored', you say it with her.

She stops. The fingers stay up. 'You know about the thesis.' It is not a question, and you both let it not be one.

'Then you know what I want,' she says. 'Skip the speech. Is the quill still there?'

choices.label: It's still there. Two inches above your margin.
choices.resultText: She exhales eleven years of waiting in one breath. 'Fourth chance,' she says. 'Right. Planning.'

title: Through the Edge
body:
Only you can bring someone through the bubble's edge. Wren has known this for a while and has asked, carefully, exactly once. And now she is standing at the threshold with her hands jammed in her pockets so you cannot see them shaking.

Inside, the Academy holds its long breath: chalk dust hanging like weather, ten thousand books mid-flight, the feast still warm. Wren walks the corridor of her third washout without a word (her, without a word) and stops at the examiner's desk. Her thesis. The quill, two inches above the margin, forever about to write.

'Don't tell me what it was going to say,' she whispers. 'Nobody knows yet. That means it isn't wrong yet.'

choices.label: Stand with her until she's ready to leave
choices.resultText: It takes an hour. When she walks out through the edge she is not lighter. She is steadier, which is better.

choices.label: Point out the margin note the examiner HAD finished: 'promising...'
choices.resultText: She reads the one completed word forty times. 'Promising,' she says. 'I can work with promising.'

title: A Fourth Specialization
body:
Wren finds you with a piece of chalk in her hand and the particular energy of a decision already made.

'The Academy had thirty-one specializations. I failed three, which statistically is barely a sample. But I've done the coursework for a thirty-second.' She gestures at the campus around you: the held Second, the relit windows, the bell that finished its note. 'This. Keeping a moment alive. There's no examiner for it, so I'm declaring: I specialize in the Anchorhold.'

She holds out the chalk. 'You're the closest thing to faculty. Sign my slate.'

choices.label: Sign it
choices.resultText: She hangs the slate on a door that has been waiting eleven years for someone to choose it. The room is hers now. The campus feels, fractionally, more like a school.

choices.label: Sign it, and grade her thesis 'correct'
choices.resultText: 'You don't have the authority,' she says, beaming, taking the slate back before you can change either verdict. 'But I'm keeping the grade.'

title: The Fights He Won't Fight
body:
Corvin has said perhaps thirty words this expedition, and then the column with the broken-seal banners crossed the far ridge and he said none at all, just stood down, the way he does, until they passed.

Tonight he sits across the fire and spends his words like a man paying a debt.

'I was one of them. Keepers. I left the morning I heard my own mouth say a phrase I never chose. "I am only choosing where to stand."' He feeds the fire a stick. 'It wasn't mine. It was placed. I've spent every day since not finishing that sentence, because I don't know yet which half of me ends it.'

choices.label: Tell him the not-finishing IS the discipline
choices.resultText: He considers that for a long moment. 'Cheaper than a warding,' he says, which from Corvin is agreement.

choices.label: Ask what the Keepers think happened to him
choices.resultText: 'Deserter.' A shrug. 'They're not wrong. They're just not right about what I deserted.'

title: What the Cell Kept
body:
The camp is exactly where Corvin said it would be, and so is the thing he came for: his old cell's muster roll, kept the way the Keepers keep everything: reverently, and without understanding.

'My name's still on it,' he says. 'Written in my hand. That's the problem.' He watches the tents the way a man watches weather. 'The Astrologer reads what's written. A name, in my own hand, in HIS people's keeping. That's a sentence I left lying around half-finished. I want it back.'

Getting it is quiet work, and Corvin is very good at quiet. What he needs from you is simpler: stand where he can see you. An anchor, while he walks into his old life.

choices.label: Stand the anchor. Let him do it his way
choices.resultText: He is gone forty minutes and returns with one page and no sound behind him. He burns his name that night, watching it the whole way down. 'Shorter roll,' he says.

choices.label: Go in with him
choices.resultText: Two are louder than one, and the last stretch is a sprint, but he gets the page, and when he burns it, he lets you watch. From Corvin, that is a door opened.

title: The Sentence, Finished
body:
Corvin finds you on the campus wall at dusk. He has brought nothing and is carrying it like a burden anyway.

'Something you should hear.' He faces the frozen skyline. 'The phrase came back this morning. In my head, in my voice: "I am only choosing..."' He stops. And you feel it before you name it. The cadence is wrong, borrowed, a diction you have heard in corrupted mouths across four kingdoms.

He knows. That is the terrible, steady thing about Corvin: he knows exactly what is living in his mouth, and he has brought it here, to the one place the sky cannot read, to finish it.

choices.label: Let him finish it
choices.resultText: 'I am choosing where to stand,' he says, in his own cadence, every word placed like a stone. 'Here.' The sentence ends. Nothing borrowed remains in it. He breathes like a man set down.

choices.label: Finish it WITH him
choices.resultText: 'Here,' you say together, and if the sky ever reads this sentence it will find two hands on it, and no room to write between them.

title: The Sentence, Interrupted
body:
You know this evening. You have lived its shape before, in a rendering that no longer happened: Corvin on the wall, the phrase rising, the borrowed cadence about to land.

So you speak first.

'Corvin. You're about to hear the phrase. When it comes, it isn't yours, and you already ended it once. I was there.'

He stares at you for a long moment. Whatever was rising in his throat subsides, unspoken, unfed. 'It doesn't land the same,' he says slowly, 'when a man's expecting it.' The relapse becomes, instead, a quiet evening on a wall, which is all he ever wanted from one.

choices.label: Finish the sentence together, early, on your own terms
choices.resultText: 'I am choosing where to stand. Here.' Said calm, said early, said twice, once by each of you. The words hold. They were never going to do anything else.

title: The Notebook
body:
Miro has been building up to this for two days, which for Miro is an eternity of tact.

'I need to show you something and I need you to not be weird about it.' The notebook is fletcher's vellum, wrapped twice in oilcloth. 'Every year, same night, I dream about a stranger. Since I was small. I wrote them down.'

He doesn't open it. He recites: dates, details. The year you chose your school. The colour of a cloak you lost two timelines ago. A name you honored on a grave the world no longer contains.

'It's you,' he says. 'It was always you. Please explain why I know things that never happened.'

choices.label: Tell him the truth: the sky re-reads itself, and something of him listens through
choices.resultText: He is quiet for a long time. 'So the dreams are... marginalia.' He hugs the notebook. 'I'm marginalia. Okay. Okay. That's... I'm going to need a day.'

choices.label: Ask to read all of it
choices.resultText: There are more entries than there have been timelines. Some describe renderings even you don't remember. You do not tell him which ones.

title: The Question No Native Asks
body:
Past the campfire's reach, Miro asks it plainly, the way he has clearly rehearsed.

'When the sky re-reads itself. When your timeline ends and the next draft starts.' He keeps his eyes on the dark. 'Where do I go?'

Every comforting answer you own is a lie, and he would know it. He has the notebook; he catches details. What he is really asking is whether anyone will know the difference between the Miro of this rendering and the next one. Whether the difference is even real.

The fire pops. He waits. He deserves whatever you actually believe.

choices.label: 'I don't know. But I remember every one of you, and the remembering is real.'
choices.resultText: He nods slowly. 'A reader remembers,' he says at last. 'That's more than most sentences get.' It is not comfort. It is something sturdier.

choices.label: 'The Hall can hold one person through the unmake. It could be you.'
choices.resultText: He goes very still. 'One chair,' he says. 'And you'd... no. Don't answer yet. Neither of us should answer that one fast.'

title: The Question, Answered First
body:
You know what tonight is. You have sat through this fire before, in a rendering that no longer happened, and watched Miro spend three hours building the courage to ask it.

So you answer before he asks.

'You want to know where you go when the sky re-reads itself. Here's everything I actually know...' and you give him all of it: the drafts, the marginalia, the remembering, the one chair. Unrehearsed on his side, honest on yours.

He listens the whole way through with the notebook clutched to his chest. 'You've answered this before,' he says finally. 'For me. Some other me.' A slow, wondering grin. 'I ask GOOD questions.'

choices.label: The best in any rendering
choices.resultText: Prepared lands better than surprised. The compendium of him, updated. He sleeps easily, which the other Miro did not.

title: Choosing to Matter
body:
Miro is waiting at the campus gate with his pack, the notebook, and a decision.

'I did the maths. If the sky re-reads itself, being careful doesn't save me. The next draft just gets a careful Miro it never met.' He plants the pack by the gatehouse. 'So I'm done being a background detail. I want the gate post. First face anyone sees walking into the one place the sky can't read. If some other rendering of me is going to inherit my life, I want him inheriting THIS one.'

He squares up, self-appointed, entirely serious. 'Also I already moved my stuff in. This is a courtesy meeting.'

choices.label: Confirm the post: the gate is his
choices.resultText: He salutes with the wrong hand, corrects it, and takes up the watch. The campus gains a gatekeeper who dreams true. It has, you suspect, always had one. The drafts just kept misplacing him.

choices.label: Point out the gate already feels like his
choices.resultText: 'It DOES, right?' He pats the arch. 'Maybe the other drafts knew. Maybe I always end up here.' He grins. 'Good. Let the sky copy THAT forward.'

title: The Audit
body:
Seraphine falls into step beside you with a slim ledger you have never seen her carry and the smile of a professional about to present findings.

'I've been annotating your deals. Habit. I was a negotiator's protégé before I was a clause.' She flips pages: your bargains, each one margin-noted in a small precise hand. 'You're good. Softer than you should be twice, sharper than you needed to be once.'

She closes the ledger. 'Here's my finding. Every deal you make, you treat both parties as people. I was traded across a table by men who laughed while they did it. So I audit everyone I work for.' A beat. 'You passed. I thought you should know the standard existed.'

choices.label: Ask which deal was 'sharper than needed'
choices.resultText: She tells you, precisely, including what it will cost you in two lunations. She is right. She is always going to be right, and you had better get used to it.

choices.label: Ask about the table she was traded across
choices.resultText: 'Good humor. A round of drinks. My apprenticeship for a shipping route.' Her voice stays level as a scale. 'They weren't cruel. That's what I want you to understand. It doesn't take cruelty. Just a contract nobody reads from the inside.'

title: The Original Instrument
body:
The archive is a notary's strongroom gone to seed, and Seraphine knows exactly which drawer. She has clearly known for years, and never come. Not alone.

The contract is one page. Her whole transfer is one page. She reads it standing very straight, one clause at a time, and you watch her negotiator's calm hold and hold and then, at the signature line, hold anyway, which is somehow worse.

'Clause four,' she says at last. 'My duties transfer. My debts transfer. My CONSENT...' she taps the blank space where no such clause exists, '...was not considered a term.' She looks up. 'I'm keeping this. What do you think: framed, or burned?'

choices.label: Framed: a standard needs an exhibit
choices.resultText: 'Framed,' she agrees. 'In my office. Facing the client's chair.' Every deal she audits for you from now on is measured against one page on a wall.

choices.label: Burned: she owes it nothing
choices.resultText: She considers the flame for a long moment, then folds the page into her ledger instead. 'No. Burning is for things with power left. This is a reference document.' It goes in under R.

title: The Original Instrument (Second Reading)
body:
This time she does not search the strongroom. She walks straight to the drawer, because this time you told her the road, having walked it in a rendering that no longer happened.

'You knew where it was,' she says, not looking up from the page. 'Which means some version of me already stood here and read this.' She taps clause four without needing to find it. 'So tell me, since you're the continuity between us: how did she take it?'

choices.label: Standing very straight. She measured it, filed it under R, and beat it.
choices.resultText: Seraphine nods once, professional to professional, to a woman who no longer happened. 'Then I'll take her result as precedent,' she says, and files it under R again, for both of them.

title: Renegotiation
body:
Seraphine books the meeting formally: a table, two chairs, her ledger squared to the grain of the wood. She has never once needed an appointment to talk to you, which is how you know what this is.

'I was transferred to this guild's predecessor-in-interest by an instrument I've now read,' she begins, crisply. 'I'm exercising a right that document never granted me: renegotiation, as a party. Not a clause.'

Her terms are on one page, in the small precise hand: her service, freely offered. Her audits, continuing. One addition. 'Item three. If the sky unmakes this arrangement, the next rendering of this table inherits my terms, not theirs.'

She sets down the pen. 'Negotiate properly. I'll know if you're being soft.'

choices.label: Sign as equals: terms accepted as drafted
choices.resultText: 'Counter-offer expected and not received. Noted with disappointment.' But she signs with the flourish of a woman writing herself into her own contract at last, party of the first part, this rendering and all that follow.

choices.label: Counter: add item four, the guild audits HER deals too
choices.resultText: Her eyes go bright. 'A reciprocal clause. NOW you're negotiating.' She initials it instantly. Being auditable, it turns out, was the thing nobody ever thought she was worth.

title: The Grove That Held
body:
The blight has circled this grove and stopped, the way water circles a stone. Inside the untouched green, a man sits against an oak with a walking staff across his knees and the look of someone at the far end of a long argument.

'Two lunations,' he says, without greeting. 'It didn't get in. I don't know what I did. I just didn't leave.' He is half-starved and entirely calm. The grove leans toward him slightly, the way rooms lean toward their oldest resident.

His name is Bram. The grove, he says, can manage without him now. He isn't sure he can say the same the other way around.

choices.label: Take him in: the guild has room for a man groves trust
choices.resultText: He stands, bows to the oak, not to you, and shoulders his pack. 'I'll want to come back,' he says. 'Groves remember who held them.'

choices.label: Leave supplies and directions to the campus
choices.resultText: He finds the campus nine days later anyway, thinner and unbothered. 'The grove said to hurry,' he explains, as if that settles anything.

title: Names, Properly
body:
Maren walks beside you with the guild's ledger of honored dead open across one arm, her own longer ledger balanced on the other, cross-referencing at a pace that would trip anyone else.

'Three errors,' she says at last. 'This one died facing the wrong way. It matters, write it. This one had a daughter; the daughter should be findable. And this one...' her finger stops. 'This one I already have. I recorded them two years before they ever met your guild.'

She closes both books. 'Your dead are kept better than most. I'd like the charge of them anyway. Nobody should be a line item in a book nobody reads.'

choices.label: Give her the charge of the guild's dead
choices.resultText: She accepts the ledger the way other people accept a rank. That night, and every night after, she reads three names before sleeping. Different three each night. She is going around the whole list.

choices.label: Ask about the one she already had
choices.resultText: She shows you the older entry: same name, a village, a kindness noted. 'Everyone is in somebody's book before they're in yours,' she says. 'I just try to be the somebody.'

title: Names, Properly (Her Own Hand)
body:
Maren opens the guild's ledger of honored dead and stops on the first page.

The marginalia is in her hand. Not similar. Hers, the particular way she crosses a seven, annotating deaths she has never read in a book she has never held. From a rendering that no longer happened.

She is quiet for a long time. 'I keep the names,' she says finally, 'so the dead stay real when nobody else remembers. It didn't occur to me somebody was doing the same for me.' She takes up the pen. 'The charge is mine, then. Apparently it always is.'

choices.label: It always is
choices.resultText: She nods once and starts reading names from her own annotations, trusting the woman who wrote them completely.

title: The Unrecorded
body:
The corrupted village is quiet in the wrong way: not empty, unwritten. The grave markers stand in rows, and the names on them are going: not weathered, RETREATING, letters unspelling themselves as the Astrologer's influence re-drafts what this place was.

Maren stands among them with her ledger and her jaw set. 'He edits,' she says. She will not use the name. 'The dead are the easiest edit. Nobody argues for them.'

She uncaps her ink. 'I argue for them. Read me the stones that still have letters. We do this fast and we do this right.'

choices.label: Read her the stones, fastest first
choices.resultText: You call names; she writes faster than the letters fade. Forty-one names cross from stone to page before the last marker goes smooth. Forty-one arguments the edit loses.

choices.label: Copy alongside her, two ledgers at once
choices.resultText: Two hands, two books, one village kept. When it's done she checks your pages for errors, finds one, corrects it without comment, and re-inks your seven the way she crosses hers.

title: The Reading
body:
Maren asks for one evening, the refectory, and everyone who can be spared. No explanation. She stands at the head of the long table with the guild's ledger and hers, side by side.

Then she reads. Every name. The guild's dead, timeline by timeline: the ones this rendering remembers and the ones only the ledger does. Where she has details, she gives one each: died facing the enemy; had a daughter; held the door.

It takes the whole evening. Nobody leaves. The frozen feast steams gently at the room's far end, patient, while the living hear out the cost of every reset, itemized.

choices.label: Stay to the last name
choices.resultText: The final name hangs in the air with the bell's long note. 'That's the ledger,' Maren says, closing it. 'Same time next year. It will be longer.' It is the closest to hopeful you have ever heard her.

choices.label: Add a name she doesn't have: one you carried alone
choices.resultText: She writes it without asking why you kept it private, adds the one detail you offer, and reads it back into the room. Carried alone no longer.

title: The Ledger, Resumed
body:
Maren sets both ledgers on the table between you, hers and the guild's, and taps the marginalia in her own hand from a rendering that no longer happened.

'We've done this,' she says. 'You, me, the reading, the whole road. The books remember even when I don't.' She uncaps her ink. 'I'm not walking the long way to a conclusion I've already signed. The dead are mine to keep. Confirmed?'

choices.label: Confirmed
choices.resultText: She re-inks the old marginalia so it holds another rendering, takes the charge of the guild's dead, and schedules the reading. The whole road, one evening: the loom already knew the way.

title: The Wage
body:
Payday at a roadside camp. Ruslan counts his share with a soldier's efficiency, keeps half, and pushes the rest back across the table like something that might bite.

'Guild fund,' he says. Same as every payday.

The fire spits. He watches you not ask, and something in him decides. 'It went home. The money. Every job, most of every wage: my mother, my brother's kids, roof for the winter.' He turns a coin over. 'Village is under it now. The corruption. Post doesn't go there. Nothing goes there.' He sets the coin down flat, precise. 'A wage with no address is just weight.'

choices.label: Hold the weight for him: the fund keeps his name on it
choices.resultText: 'Fine. But write it separate.' He watches you mark the ledger: Vane, held. Not spent. Held. It matters more than he wants it to.

choices.label: Tell him weight is what walls are made of
choices.resultText: He grunts, which is Ruslan for a whole conversation, and pockets one extra coin. 'For the wall, then. When there's a wall.'

title: Within Sight of It
body:
The route crests a ridge, and there it is: his village, in the middle distance, under corruption the way a field lies under weather. Roofs still standing. Smoke from two chimneys. People still live there, in the Astrologer's marches, because leaving is its own kind of dying.

Ruslan stops walking. He does not go closer, and no one suggests it.

'Second chimney from the well,' he says evenly. 'That one's ours.' A long silence. 'They're not dead. They're EDITED. My mother says his phrases now, probably. Thinks they're hers.' His hand finds his sword grip, and releases it. The enemy here is not a thing swords reach.

choices.label: Stand with him until he's ready to move
choices.resultText: He watches the smoke for the space of ten breaths, then turns down the far side of the ridge. 'Two chimneys,' he says, to himself, filing it. Proof of roofs. Proof of winter fires. Proof, at minimum, of holding.

choices.label: Promise him this region's corruption is on the guild's list
choices.resultText: 'Don't promise me,' he says, without heat. 'Promise the second chimney.' He walks on. From that day his fights in corrupted country have a different arithmetic. You would not want to be what stands between him and a cleansing.

title: A New Address
body:
Ruslan finds you at the campus with his wage pouch and, for the first time in living memory, something like nervousness.

'Been thinking about the weight.' He sets the pouch down. 'Money with no address. Except there's an address now.' He nods at the campus around you: the lit refectory, the bell that finished its note. 'This place holds. When the sky tears it up and re-deals, this place is still here. That's the only roof I know of that the weather can't reach.'

'So it goes here. The fund proper. And when you cleanse my province (when, not if), the campus pays for the first roofs. That's the address. Mine, theirs, whoever needs one.'

choices.label: Accept the terms: the Vane fund builds roofs
choices.resultText: He shakes on it, once, hard. Lighter by a pouch and by something else. Every payday after, the ledger line reads Vane: roofs, pending.

choices.label: Match it from the guild's coffers
choices.resultText: He stares at the doubled entry, then laughs, an alarming, unpracticed sound. 'Then it's a proper fund. Half the wage was always the easy part.'

title: A New Address (Already Known)
body:
Ruslan sets his wage pouch down at the campus with none of the nervousness you remember from a rendering that no longer happened.

'I know what I'm about to do,' he says. 'Don't know how I know. The pouch knows the way to the table.' He slides it over. 'Roofs fund. You match it, if the pattern holds.' A beat. 'The pattern holds, doesn't it. Somewhere you remember, we already shook on this.'

choices.label: The pattern holds. Shake on it again.
choices.resultText: 'Good,' he says, and shakes once, hard, the same grip across two renderings. Some sentences the sky insists on. Some, a man insists on right back.

title: What Held It
body:
The grove is exactly as he left it: green, quiet, ringed by a blight-line that stops like a tide against nothing. Bram walks in and exhales two lunations of held breath.

'I used to think it was me,' he says, one hand on the oak. 'Standing here. Refusing.' He shakes his head slowly. 'It wasn't. Watch.'

He steps outside the ring. The grove... attends. There is no other word for it: the way the leaves angle after him, the way the blight-line tenses. He steps back in and the whole green settles like a dog that found its person.

'It held ME,' he says. 'I just gave it a reason to bother.'

choices.label: Ask the grove how, properly, in the Druid way
choices.resultText: Bram translates the long silence that answers: it doesn't know either. It had never refused anything before. It refused because someone finally stayed to see whether it could. Wanting a witness, it turns out, is not only a human thing.

choices.label: Give it a reason to keep bothering: pledge the guild to this ground
choices.resultText: Bram relays the pledge with his palm flat on the oak. The blight-line, over the following lunation, retreats the width of one furrow. It is showing off, he says. Groves are terrible about praise.

title: What Held It (It Remembers)
body:
The grove starts leaning toward you both before you clear the treeline, before it could possibly know you were coming, unless it knew you were coming.

Bram stops at the blight-line and laughs under his breath. 'It remembers. The sky redealt the whole world and this one acre kept its notes.' The oak's shade falls across the exact spot where, in a rendering that no longer happened, you pledged the guild to this ground.

'No point asking it how it held, then,' Bram says. 'It'll just say what it said before.' He puts his palm on the bark anyway, for the pleasure of the answer.

choices.label: Renew the pledge on the remembered spot
choices.resultText: The blight-line gives back a furrow's width on the spot, no lunation of deliberation this time. Groves are terrible about praise, and worse about reunions.

title: Seedlings
body:
Bram stands at the bubble's edge with a cloth roll of cuttings from the grove and a question he has clearly lost sleep over.

'Inside the Second, nothing grows. Nothing dies either.' He unrolls the cloth: six green slips, patient. 'If I plant them in there, are they safe, or are they prisoners? A moment that holds you forever...' he looks up at the frozen campus, at everything it keeps, '...I genuinely cannot tell if that's shelter. And I'm the one who's supposed to know what green things want.'

He waits. He wants a gardener's answer or a jailer's, and he trusts you to know which one you're giving.

choices.label: Plant them at the edge: half in the Second, half in the world
choices.resultText: Rooted across the boundary, the cuttings become the only living things anywhere that both grow AND keep. Bram checks them daily and says nothing, which is how he prays.

choices.label: Shelter is a cage that loves you. Plant them inside.
choices.resultText: He plants all six in the courtyard's held light. They do not grow. They do not fade. They simply are: six green commas in the world's long sentence. He decides he can live with commas.

title: The Second Grove
body:
Bram fetches you without explanation, which from him means everything.

The cuttings have made their decision. Where they stand, the Second has... adjusted. A pocket of campus air where the stillness breathes. New leaves, small ones, the first NEW anything inside the held moment: not frozen, not racing, growing at the pace of a place that has all the time there is.

'A second grove,' Bram says. His voice does the thing it did at the first one. 'The anchor holds the campus. The campus holds them. They held anyway.' He kneels, checks the soil out of habit, and finds it perfect, out of gratitude.

'I stayed to see whether a grove could refuse,' he says. 'Now one's staying for me.'

choices.label: Name it the Thistlewade Grove
choices.resultText: He objects for form's sake and carves no sign, but the guild calls it that anyway, and he is never anywhere else at dusk.

choices.label: Let it name itself in time
choices.resultText: 'That's the right answer,' he says, relieved. 'They pick their own names. Takes about forty years.' He settles in, visibly, for the wait. Inside the Second, forty years is no obstacle at all.

title: The Grove, Resumed
body:
Bram meets you with a cloth roll of cuttings already prepared and the calm of a man skipping to a known ending.

'The grove leaned at me this morning like it had minutes of a meeting I missed,' he says. 'And I know what these want...' he taps the cuttings, '...the way you know a road you've walked. Grove at the edge. Green in the Second. Me at dusk.' He shoulders the roll. 'Some plantings the sky re-deals, and some plantings hold. Shall we skip to the holding?'

choices.label: Skip to the holding
choices.resultText: Grove visited, cuttings planted, dusk kept: the remembered road walked in an afternoon. The second grove takes faster this time, like soil that recognizes the seed.

title: The Old Route
body:
Half a day out, Dagny stops calling terrain by its features and starts calling it by name. Miller's rise. The wet cut. Second ford, the one that lies.

'Twelve years on this route,' she says, when she catches you noticing. 'Thornhelm and daughters, four wagons, spring and fall. I know where it floods, where it narrows, where the toll-men pretend not to live.' Her pace never changes; her feet are twelve years certain.

At the crest she stops. 'Then the family sold it. Route, contracts, schedule. The buyer got the maps.' A beat. 'I wasn't on the maps. Twelve years, and I was filed under equipment they didn't need to convey.'

choices.label: Their maps are worthless without what's in her head
choices.resultText: 'That's the joke,' she agrees. 'The route was never the road. It was knowing which ford lies.' She walks on, and the expedition moves faster all day, riding twelve years of someone else's diligence.

choices.label: Ask what she'd have wanted: a share? a farewell?
choices.resultText: She thinks about it for a full mile. 'A sentence,' she says finally. 'One sentence acknowledging I existed. The money I earned. The sentence they owed.'

title: The Buyer
body:
The waystation is busy, and there, tallying crates with a courteous, forgettable face, is the man who bought Dagny's route. She spots him instantly. Her hand does not go to her weapon, which somehow makes it worse.

The confrontation she has carried for two years dies in the walking of ten paces, because the buyer looks up, recognizes her, and is DELIGHTED.

'Thornhelm's guard! You're famous. Every waystation ledger has margin notes about you. I offered to keep you on, you know. The family said you'd already gone.' He says it kindly, factually. He is not a villain. Nobody in this story is a villain. That was never the shape of the wound.

Dagny stands very still, re-filing two years of anger that suddenly has no address.

choices.label: Give her the moment: say nothing
choices.resultText: 'They told him I'd gone,' she repeats, on the road after. 'They didn't even sell me. They LOST me. Like a strap. Like a buckle.' A long silence. 'Better, somehow. A buckle can walk off and guard something worth twelve years.'

choices.label: Tell the buyer what the margin notes were worth
choices.resultText: You itemize her, briefly: fords that lie, floods, toll-men. The buyer's face does honest arithmetic and lands on awe. 'That was never in the purchase,' he admits. Dagny stands a little differently the rest of the day.

title: The Buyer (The Words Ready)
body:
You have watched this meeting go sideways before, in a rendering that no longer happened. You watched two years of anger find no address and have to be re-filed on the road.

So this time, at the waystation door, you tell her what's coming: he's courteous. He offered to keep you on. They said you'd already gone.

Dagny receives it like a scouting report, which is to say professionally, and with one long breath. Then she walks the ten paces with the words already chosen.

'I'm the margin notes,' she tells the buyer, before he can be delighted at her. 'The family lost me like a buckle. Their error. I guard a campus now: the one address the weather can't reach.' She sets a Thornhelm route-token on his crate: returned, with prejudice, twelve years paid in full.

choices.label: Walk out with her
choices.resultText: Prepared lands better than surprised. On the road she flips her remaining route-token, hers and the guild's, and pockets it. 'Knew the words this time,' she says. 'Wonder who I practiced on.'

title: A Route of Her Own
body:
Dagny has drawn a patrol route on the campus map, in pencil, apologetically, awaiting approval. It rings the grounds and the near approaches: the gate, the walls, the road in, the blind spot by the old orchard that has bothered her since arriving.

'Every worthwhile place has a route,' she says. 'Someone who walks it, spring and fall, wet and dry, until the place and the person have memorized each other.' She squares the map. 'Twelve years, I kept somebody else's. I'd like one that can't be sold out from under me.'

'The campus can't be bought. Can't be lost. Can't file me under equipment.' She holds out the pencil. 'Make it official.'

choices.label: Ink the route: the Thornhelm Round, permanent
choices.resultText: She walks it that same evening, learning her ground the way she learns everything: completely, on foot, in all weathers. Within a lunation the campus has a rhythm it did not have before: her boots at dusk, as reliable as the bell.

choices.label: Add her to the campus charter by name
choices.resultText: Dagny Thornhelm, Keeper of the Round: written, witnessed, unsellable. She reads her own name on the charter twice. 'A sentence acknowledging I existed,' she says quietly. 'Took thirteen years. Worth it.'

title: The Round, Resumed
body:
Dagny meets you with the campus map already marked, in ink this time, no apology.

'My feet know a route here,' she says. 'Gate, walls, orchard blind spot. I've never walked it, and my boots disagree.' She taps the map. 'We've done this, haven't we. Somewhere the sky shuffled away, I keep a Round here, and it can't be sold, and my name's on a charter.'

She holds out the pen, entirely certain. 'Twelve years I kept a route that forgot me. This one remembers me across the end of the world. Sign it back to me.'

choices.label: Sign it back to her
choices.resultText: The Thornhelm Round, re-inked in an afternoon: route, charter, name. Her boots take up the dusk rhythm that same night, exactly on the old beat. Some routes, once walked, stay walked.

title: The Fourth Chance, Shorthand
body:
Wren meets you with her slate already lettered and a look that dares you to make her do the whole speech again.

'Three washouts, a thesis, a frozen quill, a room I choose. We've done it. I can FEEL that we've done it; the chalk practically writes itself.' She spins the slate: her declared specialization, the Anchorhold, thirty-second of thirty-one. 'The sky redealt the world and kept my paperwork. Rude of it. Efficient, though.' She holds out the chalk. 'Faculty signature. Same as last time.'

choices.label: Sign it, same as last time
choices.resultText: Slate hung, room chosen, thesis re-graded 'promising' by executive authority. The whole arc, one corridor's walk: the fourth chance, fourth-chanced.

title: The Sentence, Kept
body:
Corvin finds you on the wall at dusk, and for once he opens his mouth without waiting a lunation.

'The words came back this morning. All of it: the fights, the roll, the borrowed cadence at the end.' He watches the frozen skyline. 'Except I know how it ends. I've ended it. Somewhere the sky shuffled away, I stood on this wall and chose.' He turns. 'A man shouldn't have to desert the same war twice. Witness it once more and be done.'

choices.label: Witness it
choices.resultText: 'I am choosing where to stand. Here.' Once, in his own cadence, unrehearsed and unhurried. A sentence so thoroughly his that no rendering can lend it out again. He nods, paid up, and goes back to his forty words a lunation.

title: The Dream, Skipped Ahead
body:
Miro is waiting at the campus gate with his pack already down and the notebook open to its last page.

'New entry this morning. Want to hear it?' He reads: 'The gate. The question. The answer about remembering. The post. You let me skip ahead this time.' He closes it, delighted and slightly smug. 'I dreamed the SHORTCUT. Do you know how rare recursive foreshadowing is? I ask the best questions and I dream the best dreams.'

He toes his pack against the gatehouse wall, already home. 'So: gate post, remembered answer, choosing to matter. Confirm?'

choices.label: Confirmed: the gate was always his
choices.resultText: The whole arc settles into place in one conversation, the way a remembered song needs only its first bar. The campus regains its dreaming gatekeeper, and the drafts stop misplacing him.

title: Renegotiation, Precedent Cited
body:
Seraphine books the table formally, then sits without her usual preamble and slides one page across: her terms, drafted, initialed, including item three, the clause about renderings, already invoked.

'Precedent,' she says. 'Somewhere the sky shuffled away, we executed this agreement. I wrote the inheritance clause specifically so the next me wouldn't have to walk the whole road again: audit, strongroom, clause four, all of it.' She sets down the pen with a small, genuine smile. 'It worked. I'm the next me. Honor the clause.'

choices.label: Honor the clause: signed as equals, again
choices.resultText: Party of the first part, this rendering and all that follow. The words hold across the end of the world, exactly as she drafted them to. She files the page under R, for precedent. Both meanings.

title: The Weight, Already Addressed
body:
Payday. Ruslan counts his share, keeps half, and then stops, pouch in hand, frowning at his own arm like it's acting on old orders.

'This goes somewhere,' he says slowly. 'The fund. The roofs. We shook on it. I can feel the handshake and I never made it.' He looks at the campus walls around you, then sets the whole pouch on the table, decision arriving ahead of the memory. 'The sky redealt the world and my wage still knows its address. Fine. Roofs fund, matched if the pattern holds, second chimney first when the province comes clean. Shake.'

choices.label: Shake: the pattern holds
choices.resultText: Once, hard, the grip that crosses renderings. The ledger line reads Vane: roofs, pending, in ink that might as well be older than the timeline. The whole road, one payday.

title: What the Mission Was
body:
The route crosses an old burn scar, years old, regrown at the edges, dead at the heart. Elara stops walking like she's hit a wall only she can see.

'Charter mission,' she says, eventually. 'Enforcement clause nine: deny the enemy the crossing. There was a village at the crossing.' Her jaw works. 'I called the storm to the ford like the charter said. Fire found the thatch. The charter had a clause for the ford. It didn't have one for the thatch.'

'I burned the charter the same week. Figured one of us should know what it felt like.'

choices.label: The clause failed her. Say so.
choices.resultText: 'That's the kind thing to say.' She looks at the dead heart of the scar. 'I wrote my name under that clause, though. Kindness has to fit around that or it doesn't fit.'

choices.label: Ask what clause nine should have said
choices.resultText: She answers instantly, having had years to word it: 'Deny the crossing WITHOUT taking what can't be given back.' A beat. 'Eleven words. Nobody wrote them. That's the whole story.'

title: The Survivor
body:
The waystation keeper's assistant has a burn-slick arm, a crossing-village accent, and, the moment she sees Elara, no expression at all.

Elara doesn't run. That's the thing you'll remember: she walks straight over, storm-caller to survivor, and says, 'I called it. The fire that took your village came down my arm. I'm not here to be forgiven. I'm here so you know it wasn't weather. Somebody did it, and the somebody has a face.'

The silence stretches. The survivor studies her the way you study old wounds.

'I know,' the woman says at last. 'I've known your face for years. You're the only one who ever came back to wear it.'

choices.label: Leave them to talk. Some ledgers balance privately.
choices.resultText: They talk until the candle goes. Elara comes back hollowed out and lighter both, carrying the same weight, but properly now, with both hands.

choices.label: Stand with Elara while she listens
choices.resultText: The survivor tells the whole night, who got out and who didn't, and one thing Elara never knew: the storm-front SHE called broke first, and half the village walked out under its rain. Fire and rain, one arm. She has to sit down.

title: The Survivor (Known)
body:
You know who's at that waystation. You watched this meeting happen in a rendering that no longer happened. So on the road you tell Elara what's waiting: the burn-slick arm, the crossing accent, the sentence 'you're the only one who ever came back to wear it.'

Elara walks the last mile in silence, but it's a different silence: a rehearsal, not a dread.

At the door she turns. 'Somewhere the sky shuffled away, I already survived this conversation.' A grim, real smile. 'Then it's survivable. That's more than I've ever known walking into a room.'

choices.label: It's survivable. Go.
choices.resultText: Prepared lands better than surprised. She goes in steady, and this time when she hears about the rain her own storm gave, she's able to say thank you for it, to the storm, and to the woman who kept the accounting.

title: A Charter Worth Keeping
body:
Elara finds you with a single sheet, good paper, careful hand. A charter. Hers.

'The old one had forty clauses and I could recite them drunk. Clauses for fords, for lines, for acceptable losses.' She sets the sheet down. 'Mine has one.'

The page reads, in full: *Nothing the fire can't give back.*

'Every working I call answers to that first. If a storm can't pass the clause, the storm stays in my hands.' She slides it across. 'The old charter had a guildmaster's seal to make it real. Humor me.'

choices.label: Seal it
choices.resultText: One clause, sealed and witnessed. She folds it into the lining over her heart, where enforcers keep their charters. The difference is that she wrote this one, and it fits.

choices.label: Seal it and adopt the clause guild-wide
choices.resultText: She stares. 'The whole guild?' Then, carefully, like handling something hot: 'Then it wasn't just an apology. It was a draft.' The clause enters the guild's standing orders in her handwriting.

title: One Clause, Recited
body:
Elara meets you with a single sheet already written. The paper knew the words before she did, she says.

'One clause. *Nothing the fire can't give back.* I've written it before. I can tell; the hand's too sure for a first draft.' She sets it down with the burn scar's story and the survivor's name, all of it delivered like a report on a road already walked. 'Somewhere the sky shuffled away, you sealed this. Seal it again. Some charters should survive the weather.'

choices.label: Seal it again
choices.resultText: The clause, resealed across the end of the world. She files the whole road (scar, survivor, charter) under settled, and her storms answer to eleven words from that day on.

title: The Itch
body:
Fenna has a diagram. Of the anchor. The thing holding the campus, the Second, and arguably the world.

'Request to dismantle,' she says brightly. 'Non-destructively! Mostly. There's a contingency appendix.' The appendix is thicker than the diagram. 'I rebuilt the mill BETTER, you know. I was eleven. I've grown as a person and an engineer.'

She knows the answer. She's known the answer since she started drawing. But the mill was the first machine that ever kept a secret from her, and this one is keeping the biggest secret anyone's ever kept, and her hands itch and itch and itch.

choices.label: No. But commission the instruments: measure everything, touch nothing.
choices.resultText: 'MEASURE everything...' she repeats, already redesigning. Within a lunation the anchor has more instrumentation than the rest of the campus combined, and Fenna has readings nobody in history has had.

choices.label: Ask what she thinks is inside
choices.resultText: Her answer takes twenty minutes and four more diagrams and ends with: '...or it's a held breath, mechanically speaking, and you can't dismantle a breath, which is EXACTLY why I want to try.' The no stands. The itch, visibly, becomes a vocation.

title: The Itch (Prior Readings)
body:
Fenna arrives with her dismantling request, opens the appendix, and stops. Tucked in the binding is a page of instrument readings in her own hand, dated a year this world never had.

'These are MINE. This is my notation. These are readings off the ANCHOR...' she flips pages faster and faster, '...someone let me instrument it. Someone smart. Someone about to be asked again.'

She looks up with the expression of a woman skipping four drafts of an argument.

choices.label: Commission the instruments, again, apparently
choices.resultText: 'Continuity of research!' she crows, and has the array rebuilt in half the time, checking her own ghost's readings as she goes. They match. Across the end of the world, they match. She frames the old page.

title: A Broken Working
body:
The mechanism sits in a ruin: a warding engine, old make, seized mid-rotation, and around it the scars of everyone who tried force. Pry marks. Scorch. One bent crowbar, abandoned like an apology.

Fenna circles it once and sits down cross-legged. 'Everybody asks a machine to move,' she says. 'Nobody asks it why it stopped.'

She watches it for an hour. The party waits. Then: 'There. Fourth gear's not jammed. It's WAITING. Something upstream promised it a signal that never came. It's been holding its half of a bargain for two hundred years.' She takes out one small tool. 'We're not going to force it. We're going to keep the promise.'

choices.label: Keep the promise: send the signal
choices.resultText: One tap on the right contact: the engine takes a breath two centuries deep and turns over, wards blooming like frost in reverse. Fenna pats it once. 'Good lad. Sorry about the crowbar people.'

choices.label: Ask what it was warding
choices.resultText: She traces the ward-lines outward to a collapsed cellar the ruin kept safe this whole time: records, intact, two hundred years dry. 'Machines keep their promises,' she says. 'It's their whole personality.'

title: Maintenance
body:
Fenna requests a meeting, which is unlike her. She usually just appears, mid-sentence.

'I withdraw the dismantling request. Formally. Forever.' She sets down a new document, thin, one page, no appendix. 'The mill taught me you learn a machine by taking it apart. The anchor taught me the other thing. Some works you learn by TENDING. You maintain them for thirty years and at the end you know things no dismantler could.'

The page is a maintenance charter: inspection rounds, instrument logs, one line at the bottom in her tidiest hand: *machinist to the held moment.*

'It's the best machine anyone's ever built and nobody built it. Let me keep it.'

choices.label: Appoint her machinist to the held moment
choices.resultText: She signs like it's her eleventh birthday. From then on the anchor's instrument log fills daily, and the campus acquires a sound it didn't know it was missing: someone humming at the works.

choices.label: Appoint her, and ask for the mill story, the whole thing
choices.resultText: The signed charter and the whole story: nine-year-old Fenna, the mill's secret (a cracked shaft everyone had painted over), the rebuild. 'I didn't dismantle it to break it,' she says. 'I dismantled it because nobody would TELL me. The anchor tells me things. That's the difference.'

title: Machinist, Reinstated
body:
Fenna walks in with a one-page maintenance charter already drafted and her instrument case already packed.

'So here's the thing. My hands know an inspection round I've never walked. My notation has entries for gauges that aren't installed yet. Either I'm haunting myself...' she considers this, '...which is acceptable... or somewhere the sky shuffled away, I'm the machinist to the held moment, and the position is simply awaiting re-appointment.'

She holds out the charter and a pen, vibrating slightly.

choices.label: Re-appoint the machinist
choices.resultText: Signed in one stroke. The instrument array goes up in record time, the log resumes as if uninterrupted, and the anchor, she swears, settles, like a machine whose person came back.

title: The Letters
body:
Isolde lays the letter on the table like evidence, which is what it is.

Fine paper. A court wizard's hand. It arrived at a waystation three days ahead of an itinerary you finalized two days ago.

'My old patron,' she says. 'He released me from service to repay a Major favor: clean, sealed, witnessed. Except he still writes. Always ahead of me. Always PLEASED.' Her finger taps the closing line: *Your progress continues to satisfy. V.* 'Chronomancers don't watch you, you understand. They read ahead. I was his retainer for nine years and I still can't tell if I'm his correspondent...' the tap becomes a flat palm, '...or his margin note.'

choices.label: A margin note doesn't get letters. Correspondents do. Write back.
choices.resultText: She stares, then laughs, one sharp, surprised note. 'Write BACK. Nine years and it never once...' She drafts three words that evening: *Reading ahead too. I.* The next letter arrives visibly rattled. She frames it.

choices.label: Ask what the favor was that bought her freedom
choices.resultText: 'That's the thing.' Her voice goes careful. 'I don't know. Someone spent a Major favor, the kind you only ever get one of, on releasing a retainer he'd barely miss. I've been trying to work out who paid for me, and what they think they bought.'

title: The Watcher's Man
body:
Two days of the same figure at the edge of sight, never closer, never gone. On the third morning Isolde pours two cups of tea and walks out of camp without a word of explanation, straight to a copse nobody else had marked.

'You're using my spacing,' she tells the copse. 'Third-remove, sightline discipline. I WROTE that discipline. Come have your tea.'

The watcher who emerges is young, mortified, and, at the sight of her, reverent. Her replacement. Sent not to spy, he insists, but to LEARN: the patron said *follow the Marrec method as far as it goes.*

Isolde's face does several things she would deny under oath.

choices.label: Let her decide what to do with her disciple
choices.resultText: She spends the evening correcting his technique, brutally, thoroughly, fondly, then sends him home with a sealed critique addressed to the patron: *The method goes further than you'll ever read. Stop sending students. Send tuition.*

choices.label: Offer the boy an honest apprenticeship: the guild pays better
choices.resultText: The watcher defects on the spot, which Isolde declares 'sloppy loyalty, excellent judgment.' The patron's next letter contains, for the first time in nine years, a question rather than an assessment. She does not answer it.

title: Released, Properly
body:
Isolde asks you to walk her through the bubble's edge, into the Second, the one place the sky cannot read ahead.

Inside, in the held light of the frozen campus, she takes out nine years of letters. The whole correspondence, kept in oilcloth, carried through everything.

'He reads ahead,' she says. 'Every reply I ever drafted, he'd answered before I sent it. But in HERE...' she looks up at the hanging chalk dust, the stopped bell, '...there is no ahead. Whatever I do in this room, he reads it never.'

She builds a small, neat fire in a brazier that has been about to be lit for eleven years, and feeds it the first letter. 'Witness it. That's all I need. One witness the sky can't overrule.'

choices.label: Witness the burning, every letter
choices.resultText: Nine years, letter by letter, ash by ash, in a moment the Astrologer will never turn to. When it's done she pockets one blank sheet of his fine paper ('severance pay') and walks out through the edge lighter than the smoke.

choices.label: Suggest she keep one: the first
choices.resultText: She reads the first letter a long moment. *You will do well. You always were going to. V.* Then she burns it last of all. 'Especially this one. Nobody gets to have always-known me. Not even kindly.'

title: Released, Properly (The Ash Remembers)
body:
Isolde stands at the bubble's edge with the oilcloth packet of letters and a frown of professional suspicion.

'I counted them this morning. Nine years of letters, and ash smudges on the oilcloth I never made. My hands remember a fire.' She looks at you. 'We burned these. In there, where he can't read. And the sky redealt the world and put them back in my bag, but it couldn't redeal the SMUDGE. He missed a spot.'

Her smile is thin and bright as a knife. 'Chronomancer error. I intend to compound it.'

choices.label: Compound it: burn them again, same brazier
choices.resultText: Second verse, same fire, same witness. Ash twice over across two renderings, a correspondence so thoroughly ended that even the sky's own filing cannot retrieve it. She keeps the smudged oilcloth as a trophy: proof the read-ahead has a margin, and she lives in it.

title: The Release, Executed
body:
Isolde meets you with the oilcloth packet and a single prepared statement, delivered in the tone of a woman executing a will.

'The letters. The watcher. The fire in the Second. I've done it. The smudges on this oilcloth are mine and I never made them. So we skip to the end: you walk me through the edge, I burn nine years where the sky can't read, one witness, no speeches.' A beat. 'Slightly fewer speeches.'

choices.label: Walk her through. Witness. No speeches.
choices.resultText: Fire, ash, one blank sheet of fine paper pocketed as severance. The whole release executed in an afternoon, precedent cited. On the way out she says, to the frozen sky generally: 'Read THAT ahead.'

title: How He Counts
body:
'Three more rounds of this hill,' Kael says, and it's the fourth time today he's counted something in rounds, so someone finally asks.

He grins, which is how he handles everything, and then doesn't grin, which is how you know this is real.

'The pit. They summoned a thing with a furnace where the heart goes. Elemental. Crowd paid triple.' He rolls his shoulder, the one with the burn-scar map. 'Three rounds I stood up. Bell, bell, bell. Then the summoner got bored and un-summoned it.' He taps his temple. 'Un-summoned. Not killed. It's still out there in whatever room the summoned wait in. And here's the thing about that fight. Nobody rang the last bell. By pit rules?' The grin comes back sideways. 'We're still fighting.'

choices.label: By pit rules, he's owed a round four
choices.resultText: 'THANK you.' He points at you like you've settled a nine-year argument. 'Everyone says let it go. You don't LET GO of an open round. You train for it.' He does one more circuit of the hill, for form.

choices.label: Ask what the crowd saw in round three
choices.resultText: 'A man who wouldn't fall down,' he says simply. 'That's all standing up is, third round against a furnace. It's not winning. It's refusing to make it easy.' He says it like a creed, because it is one.

title: Round Four
body:
The manifestation site is still smoking: furnace-heat shimmer, glass where grass was, and in the middle of it, turning at your approach with an almost human deliberation, the elemental. His elemental. Nine years older and not one degree cooler.

It sees Kael and stops.

He walks forward, rolling his shoulders, unhurried as a man returning to his seat. 'Hey, big lad.' His voice is easy; his stance is not. 'They pulled you before the bell. That's on them, not us.' He raises his fists. 'Round four. Winner rings it this time.'

The furnace-heart bellows. You'd swear it sounds glad.

choices.label: Ring them in: fight it beside him
choices.resultText: Round four runs long and loud, and ends with Kael landing the last blow and CATCHING the elemental's guttering core before it hits the ground, setting it down gently, like a beaten opponent's arm you raise. 'Good rounds,' he tells it. 'All four.' The bell, when you strike the old ward-chime nearby, rings clean.

choices.label: Hold the crowd's job: witness, count, ring the bell
choices.resultText: He fights it alone, the way it started, but with a bell this time, and a count, and a witness. It goes down in the fourth and he sits down next to where it faded, breathing hard, at peace. 'Closed match,' he says. 'Took nine years to find the bell.'

title: Round Four (He Knows the Ending)
body:
At the shimmer's edge, Kael stops, and laughs, low and wondering.

'I've fought this round.' He flexes the scarred shoulder. 'Muscle knows it. Somewhere the sky shuffled away, we rang the bell, big lad, and here you are anyway, wanting the rematch of the rematch.' The elemental's furnace-heart huffs, and Kael's grin goes warm. 'Yeah. Me too.'

He steps in with none of the nine-year weight, just craft, and something that has stopped being vengeance and started being respect.

choices.label: Ring them in for the exhibition match
choices.resultText: It's not a grudge this time; it's a bout: clean rounds, showman's pacing, the elemental playing to a crowd of one rendering's memory. It goes down in the fourth, on purpose, you'd almost swear. The bell rings clean twice: once for now, once for the fight the sky mislaid.

title: The Bell, Not the Pit
body:
Kael has been standing under the campus bell for the better part of an hour, which for Kael is a geological era of stillness.

'The bell,' he says, when you join him. 'It rings when the guild does something that matters. Shard recovered. Archmage settled. Milestones.' He looks up at it. 'The pit had a bell too. Only thing in that place that was honest. It didn't care who was winning. It just told the truth about time.'

He turns. 'I want to train the recruits. Footwork, falling down, standing up: pit knowledge, minus the pit. And when they pass, THIS bell rings for them. First honest bell some of them will ever hear.'

choices.label: Give him the training yard and the bell
choices.resultText: The Ashblade drills become campus legend: brutal, hilarious, weirdly kind. When his first class passes, he rings the bell himself and stands under it grinning, a man whose count finally came out even.

choices.label: Ask him to teach the third-round lesson first
choices.resultText: 'Refusing to make it easy,' he agrees. 'Lesson one, not lesson last. Everything else is footwork.' He chalks it over the training yard gate, misspelled, immortal.

title: All Four Rounds, Called
body:
Kael meets you rolling his shoulder like a man limbering for a fight already won.

'Body remembers a bout the calendar says never happened. Big lad, four rounds, a bell rung clean. And a training yard. And a chalk sign I definitely misspelled.' He grins. 'Sky redealt the deck. Fine. I've fought this whole card before. Call it, and I'll fight it again in an afternoon.'

choices.label: Call the card
choices.resultText: The elemental found, the fourth round rung, the yard claimed, the sign re-misspelled on principle. The whole count settled by dusk. 'Even,' he declares, under the bell. 'Again.'

title: The Ledger Entry
body:
Ondrej requests ten minutes and arrives with his secondment papers squared to the table edge, the way he squares everything.

'Article of transfer,' he says. 'One adept, seconded to the guild for the duration of the alliance. Signed by Master Pendry. Countersigned by nobody, because line items don't countersign.'

He folds his hands. 'I treat every spell like a ledger entry because ledgers don't lie about what things cost. So, plainly: I am entered in the Circle's books as an asset on loan, and in yours as... what? I have checked. Your books don't say.' He waits, a man who has done the accounts on himself and found a blank where the total goes.

choices.label: Enter him as guild: a member, not a loan
choices.resultText: He takes out a pen, writes MEMBER in the blank on his own copy, initials it, and files it, visibly recalibrating nine assumptions. 'Then the accounts disagree,' he says. 'Good. I know which book I keep.'

choices.label: Ask what HE wants the entry to read
choices.resultText: A long pause, the first unbudgeted pause you've seen from him. 'Present by choice,' he says finally. 'No ledger has a column for it. I've always thought that was a flaw in ledgers.'

title: Due Diligence
body:
The ruin's old working is miscasting: a containment lattice shedding arcs, cascade building. Doctrine is unambiguous, and Ondrej recites it flatly while already rolling up his sleeves: 'Circle procedure: withdraw to safe distance. Document the failure. Report.'

The guild's people are inside the lattice radius, hauling a pinned scout.

'Procedure assumes the observer has no one in the blast column,' he continues, in the exact tone of a man annotating a text, and walks INTO the radius, hands weaving counter-figures. 'Amendment, Vael, field edition: the observer has people. Beginning stabilization. Someone document ME.'

choices.label: Anchor his counter-working: buy him the seconds
choices.resultText: Between your anchor and his arithmetic the cascade dies four feet short of the scout. Ondrej stands in the discharge scar, singed and satisfied, and produces a notebook. 'Failure documented,' he says. 'Also prevented. The Circle can pick which report to file.'

choices.label: Get the scout out while he holds it
choices.resultText: He holds the lattice alone for eleven seconds (you count, because he counts, aloud, steady as a metronome) and lets it collapse the instant the scout clears. 'Doctrine says withdraw,' he says, sitting down abruptly. 'I withdrew. Eleven seconds late. Note the amendment.'

title: The Revision
body:
Ondrej has drafted a petition. Of course he has. It is addressed to Master Aurel Pendry, Archmage of the Annotated Circle, and it is two sentences long, which, for a document going to the man who revises everything, is either suicide or genius.

He reads it aloud: '*Petition to revise the article of transfer: strike "seconded for the duration." Enter "transferred, freely, permanent."* '

He sets down the page. 'He'll revise it. He revises everything. But he taught me this himself: a correction is an argument, and you can only argue with what someone actually wrote.' A breath. 'So I wrote what I am. Witness it before it goes. If the revision comes back unkind, I want it on record what the original said.'

choices.label: Witness it and send it
choices.resultText: The reply comes in eight days: the petition returned, annotated in the Reviser's own hand. *Strike "freely." Redundant; no other basis was ever entered. Approved.* Ondrej reads it four times, then frames it, redundancy and all.

choices.label: Add the guild's countersignature first
choices.resultText: Line items don't countersign. Members do. Your signature goes under his, and the reply, when it comes, is one annotation: *Ledgers reconciled. A.P.* Ondrej declares it the finest bookkeeping of his life.

title: The Revision (Anticipated)
body:
Ondrej unfolds his two-sentence petition, and stops. In the margin, in Aurel Pendry's unmistakable shorthand, an annotation is ALREADY there, on a page Ondrej wrote this morning.

*You have petitioned this before, in a draft the sky discarded. The approval carries forward. Stop wasting paper. A.P.*

Ondrej sits very still. 'He revises across RENDERINGS,' he says at last, somewhere between horror and religious awe. 'The transfer is... already entered. Was always entered.' He looks up. 'I need this witnessed anyway. Ledgers require witnesses. Even the impossible ones.'

choices.label: Witness the impossible entry
choices.resultText: Witnessed: one adept, transferred freely and permanently, approved before it was asked, in a hand that argues with the sky's own drafts. Ondrej files it under the only heading that fits: present by choice.

title: Accounts, Carried Forward
body:
Ondrej lays out his secondment papers, his petition, and a fresh page: a summary sheet, prepared in advance, because of course it is.

'The accounts are familiar,' he says. 'I have audited myself and found a prior balance: member, not loan; the amendment in the field; a petition approved in shorthand I recognize. Somewhere the sky discarded, all of this is already entered.' He slides the summary across. 'Ledger practice for a reopened book: carry the balance forward, one witness. You.'

choices.label: Carry the balance forward
choices.resultText: One signature and the whole arc reconciles: member, amendment, transfer, all re-entered in an afternoon. 'Present by choice,' he notes at the bottom. 'Balance stable across renderings.' It is, from Ondrej, poetry.

title: Seventeen
body:
Sable cleans her kit by the fire with the economy of someone who has done it ten thousand times, and then, unprompted, which means she's been building to it, starts counting.

'One through five are my father's. Snares. Poacher's basics.' A blade turns over in her hands. 'Six through eleven I worked out myself, king's forests, staying fed. Twelve through seventeen I learned the years I'm not proud of, from people you pay in advance.'

She holsters the blade. 'Seventeen ways to end something before it knows I exist. People think the number's a boast.' Her eyes stay on the fire. 'It's an inventory. I keep it current so I always know exactly what I'm choosing NOT to do.'

choices.label: Ask why the list stopped at seventeen
choices.resultText: A long silence. 'Because eighteen looked at me,' she says finally. 'Mid-stalk, perfect wind, dead to rights, and it turned its head and LOOKED. Knew I was there the whole time. Let me choose.' She banks the fire. 'I chose. List stopped.'

choices.label: An inventory of restraint is a strange kind of honor. Say so.
choices.resultText: 'Strange is right.' Almost a smile. 'Every trade's got its saints. Poachers get the patron saint of the shot not taken.' She says it mocking. She touches her kit like a reliquary.

title: The One That Saw Her
body:
The territorial sign is old and deliberate: bark stripped at a height nothing local stands, ground scored in patterns too regular for accident. Sable reads it the way others read a letter.

'It's hers,' she says quietly. 'The eighteenth.' 

The beast that comes out of the treeline is grey at the muzzle now, massive, moving with an old predator's economy, and it stops at twenty paces exactly, the same distance as that day, and looks at Sable the same way: fully aware, entirely unafraid, waiting to see what gets chosen.

Sable's hands stay off her kit. 'Twenty paces, wind to her, my move,' she murmurs. 'She's re-running it. She wants to know if I meant it.'

choices.label: Let Sable answer: hands empty, one step forward
choices.resultText: One step, empty hands, held eyes. The beast considers this for a long moment, then dips its grey muzzle once, the smallest nod in the world, and withdraws. Sable breathes out ten years. 'She meant it too,' she says. 'All this time. Both of us keeping one appointment.'

choices.label: Stand very still and witness the parley of predators
choices.resultText: Nothing moves for a full minute: two professionals reviewing an old contract. Then the beast turns and leaves the territory OPEN, unscored, hers to Sable: a hunting-right granted between equals. Sable never hunts it. That was the entire point.

title: The One That Saw Her (Both Remember)
body:
The beast is waiting at the treeline before Sable even finds the sign, already at twenty paces, already watching, grey muzzle raised in what can only be called recognition.

Sable stops dead. 'She's not re-running the old day,' she says slowly. 'She's re-running the LAST one. The step. The nod.' Her voice drops to wonder. 'The sky redealt the world and the appointment kept. Both of us. Across all of it.'

She steps forward, empty-handed, no hesitation this time. A ritual now, not a question.

choices.label: Witness the appointment, kept twice
choices.resultText: One step, one nod, two renderings deep. The beast withdraws leaving the ground open, and Sable stands in her granted territory awhile. 'Seventeen ways to end things,' she says. 'One way to keep them. Better ratio than it sounds.'

title: Warden, Not Poacher
body:
Sable unrolls a hand-drawn map of the campus grounds across the table, annotated in seventeen colors.

'Every way to kill something unseen is a way to SEE something unseen,' she says. 'Approach lines. Blind angles. Wind shadows. The seventeen, run backwards.' Her finger walks the perimeter. 'Snare-points become tripwire alarms. Stalk-lanes become patrol blinds. The rush lane by the orchard, that's how I'd come in, so that's where the bell-wire goes.'

She straightens. 'My father poached because wardens owned the seeing and we owned the hunger. I want to own the seeing, for a place that feeds people. Full circle, run backwards. Say yes.'

choices.label: Yes: the grounds are hers to ward
choices.resultText: Within two lunations the campus perimeter is a marvel nobody can see: seventeen quiet countermeasures, each one a killing method retired into a warning. Nothing approaches unannounced again. Dagny's Round and Sable's web, it's noted, fit together like they were drawn by one hand.

choices.label: Yes, and ask her to teach the seeing to the scouts
choices.resultText: Her course has one rule, chalked at the yard: FIRST KNOW WHERE YOU'D COME IN. The scouts emerge paranoid and precise. Sable emerges, to her open suspicion, happy.

title: The Web, Rewoven
body:
Sable arrives with the seventeen-color map already drawn, corrections included, in her own hand, for defenses that were never built.

'I inventoried the grounds this morning,' she says. 'Found myself checking a bell-wire that doesn't exist. By the orchard. Where I'd come in.' She taps the map. 'We've woven this web before, somewhere the sky shuffled away. The appointment with the old girl, too. My feet already know the twenty paces.' She rolls the map, businesslike. 'Approve the re-weave. It goes faster the second rendering.'

choices.label: Approve the re-weave
choices.resultText: Web rewoven, appointment kept, course rechalked: the whole territory resettled in days. The eighteenth way, it turns out, is the only one that survives the end of the world: the one where everybody walks away.

title: The Spear's Weight
body:
Third watch. Torrin sits with the spear across his knees, the way he always does, and tonight he looks down at it like he's noticed it for the first time in years.

'Nine years,' he says. 'Picked it up the night of the fire. Haven't set it down since. Eat with it in reach. Sleep with it in hand. Ask anyone who's shared a watch.' He turns it slowly. 'Good spear. Farmer's haft, soldier's head. Like me.'

He's quiet a while. 'Here's the arithmetic I did tonight: the bandits took one night from my village. I've given that same night nine YEARS of guard duty. At some point the math stopped being vigilance.' His hands don't loosen. 'Knowing it and putting it down aren't the same field, though. Not even the same weather.'

choices.label: Not tonight. But name the field it'd take.
choices.resultText: 'Ground worth working,' he says at once. He's clearly had the words ready for years. 'Somewhere that can't burn. Show me a field the fire can't reach and I'll... consider the weather.' He almost smiles. The spear stays in hand. But it's the first time he's stated terms.

choices.label: Take his watch: let him sleep both hands empty, once
choices.resultText: He tries. Genuinely tries. He lies down, sets the spear ONE handspan away, and sleeps like a man on hot coals for two hours before the hand finds the haft in his sleep. In the morning he says only: 'Handspan's farther than it's been in nine years.' It counts. You both know it counts.

title: Ground Worth Working
body:
Torrin stands at the strip of earth along the campus wall, inside the Second's reach, where the light holds gold and steady, with a seed-bag so old the stitching has been repaired in three different threads.

'From home,' he says. 'Winter barley. Grabbed it the night of the fire. Don't know why. Grabbed the spear with the other hand.' He weighs the bag. 'Nine years I've carried both. Only ever used the one.'

He crouches, takes a handful of soil, does the farmer thing with his thumb that no soldier ever learns. 'Campus ground. Held ground. The fire that comes for THIS field has to get through the whole guild and one act of anchored time.' He looks up. 'That's the weather I asked you for. Requesting the plot.'

choices.label: Grant the plot: both hands in the dirt
choices.resultText: He plants the whole bag in an afternoon, spear leaned against the wall a full ten paces off, the farthest it's been since the fire. It stays in his sightline. But his hands, for one afternoon, are full of something that grows.

choices.label: Grant it, and dig the first row beside him
choices.resultText: Guildmaster and spearman, two rows, one afternoon. He talks more in that soil than in nine years of watches: the village, the fields, his father's rotation schedule. The spear leans on the wall, patient, learning to wait.

title: By the Door
body:
The barley came up. Of course it came up: held light, tended daily, planted by a man nine years hungry for the work. The strip along the wall is green going gold, and Torrin stands in it holding the spear and looking at the gatehouse.

'Made a bracket,' he says. Plain iron, by the gatehouse door, at exactly a standing man's reach. 'Not a trophy wall. Not a chest in a storeroom. BY THE DOOR.' He grips the haft, once, hard, nine years of grip in it. 'Farmer keeps his tools where the work is. If the fire ever comes for this place, the door is where I'll want it. Until then...'

He doesn't finish the sentence with words.

choices.label: Stand with him while he racks it
choices.resultText: The spear goes into the bracket with the care of a man laying something down that stayed up too long, and his hands come away, and stay away, and he stands there flexing them slowly like they're new. 'Right,' he says thickly. 'Harvest in a lunation. Bring a scythe, if you're bringing anything.'

choices.label: Point out the barley behind him: the night the fire took, given back
choices.resultText: He turns and looks at the green-gold strip a long time. 'One night taken. One field given back.' He racks the spear without ceremony, because ceremony would undo him. 'Arithmetic's even. Tell nobody I cried at MATH.'

title: By the Door (The Field Remembers)
body:
Torrin comes to find you, and for the first time in anyone's memory his hands are empty. The spear's still with him, slung, but his HANDS are empty, and he's holding something small instead.

A barley head. Full, gold, impossible.

'Growing by the wall,' he says. 'One strip. Nothing else grows in the held light, but this came up wild, exactly where a field would be if a man had planted one.' He turns it in his fingers. 'I never planted here. But somewhere the sky shuffled away... I harvested. This is MY rotation pattern. I know my own rows.'

He's already looking at the gatehouse, at the bare patch of wall beside the door exactly the size of a bracket.

choices.label: The field remembers. Finish what it started.
choices.resultText: Seed-bag planted into the ghost of its own rows; bracket forged to fit a shadow already on the wall. The spear goes down in half the time it took a lost rendering, the ground this time pulling it out of his hands.

title: The Arithmetic, Settled
body:
Torrin stands at the wall-strip with the seed-bag in one hand and the spear in the other, and he's weighing them, literally weighing them, one against the other, like scales.

'I know how this goes,' he says. 'Field here. Bracket there. Spear by the door, hands in the dirt, arithmetic even. I've DONE it. My hands know the bracket's height.' He looks over. 'Nine years I couldn't put it down once. Now I've apparently put it down twice. Third time's just practice. Witness it and hand me the scythe when it's season.'

choices.label: Witness it, and bring the scythe at harvest
choices.resultText: Planted, racked, harvested, all in remembered order. The bracket by the door holds the spear; the wall-strip holds the barley; the man holds, for the first rendering in nine years, nothing at all, by choice, with both hands.

title: What She Saw
body:
Yara has been reading the treeline all day the way clerks read contracts, and at the third crown survey marker she stops pretending it's routine.

'King's mark,' she says, thumb on the blaze. 'Resource survey. I cut a thousand of these.' Her jaw sets. 'The last season, the surveys started coming back... pre-written. Findings filled in before we walked the ground. Groves marked BLIGHTED that I'd stood in that morning, green as spring. Orders to log them anyway: quarantine timber, crown business, look the other way, Ellswood.'
